Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I spoke with Ellen Price on Tuesday, and she brought over her grandfather's envelope of photographs. The school stood near the bend where Cedar Lane meets Mill Road, and it served families from both sides of the river from 1898 until the district consolidated classes in 1936. The building was small, but it had two classrooms, a coat room, and a kitchen added later by the parent committee. Ellen says the kitchen was used for soup lunches during the winter and for preserving apples in September. Please keep that detail because it makes the school feel like a working part of the neighborhood rather than just an old building.

The photograph dated 1911 shows the east entrance and a narrow wooden ramp. The date is written on the back in pencil, along with the words “first school picnic.” The handwriting appears to be her great-aunt Clara's, but Ellen cannot confirm that, so we should say the note is in the family collection, not that Clara wrote it. There are thirteen children in the picture by my count, and perhaps a teacher standing just inside the doorway. One boy is holding a tin pail, and a little girl has a folded newspaper under her arm. We do not know why they brought either item, and I would leave that open rather than make a guess. The roofline in the image also shows a short bell tower, which does not appear in the 1924 county survey.

The school register has a different kind of evidence. Its first surviving page begins in January 1903 and lists thirty-one pupils with surnames that still appear in the local phone directory, including Bell, Ortiz, and Kerr. The teacher's name is given as Miss Ada Morrow, and a later entry calls her Miss Morrow still, so we should not assume she married during her time there. A note in the margin says two pupils walked from the ferry landing after their father was delayed at the mill. That is the only reference to the ferry in the register, but it connects the school to the river crossing that the town used before the county bridge opened in 1917.

1. The building and the record

The county survey describes a one-story frame schoolhouse with a stone foundation and a wood stove in each classroom. The survey is dated June 1924 and lists the roof as needing repair. It does not mention a bell tower or a kitchen. By then, the parent committee had already raised money for new desks and glass for the south windows. In a 1927 letter to the district clerk, committee secretary Rose Kerr asked for reimbursement of twelve dollars and forty cents for stove pipe and window putty. She wrote, “We can manage the work ourselves if the district can provide the materials.” I think that is a useful quotation because it shows how practical the committee was, but please check the original spelling before we print it. The copy Ellen gave me has a crease through the final word.

There is also a disagreement about when the school closed. The handwritten town chronology says 1935, while the district ledger records the transfer of the last pupils in September 1936. The ledger is clearer on the sequence, but it does not tell us when lessons ended for that year. I suggest we say the district consolidated the school in 1936 and avoid naming a final day unless we find another source. A notice in the Bend Weekly from October 3, 1936, says the desks were removed and stored at the town hall. That supports the transfer date without settling exactly when the doors closed.

I checked the present site on Friday with Tom Bell, who remembers visiting the property with his mother in the 1950s. There is no foundation visible from Mill Road because brush and blackberry vines cover the low ground. Tom pointed out two flat stones near the old cedar fence and said people used to call that spot the schoolyard, but he also said the fence was replaced twice, so we cannot use it to mark the original boundary. The Cedar Lane entrance is now blocked by a locked farm gate, and the current landowner asked visitors not to walk in without permission. Please make that clear in the caption if we use a location photograph.

For the layout, I would put the 1911 image beside a small map showing Cedar Lane, Mill Road, the ferry landing, and the county bridge. The map should be labeled approximate because the river channel shifted after the 1948 flood. We can ask Joel to prepare a simple version, but I have not spoken to him yet. The county archive has a 1932 road map that may help with the crossing, and Ellen says she can lend us the family photograph for one week if we arrange pickup after the fifteenth. She would prefer that we return it in a rigid sleeve rather than an envelope, and she wants her name credited as the lender, not as the owner.

I still need to confirm whether the register can be photographed. The archive volunteer said the binding is fragile and that their scanner may not open it flat. We should request permission before sending anyone with a camera, and if they decline, we can quote the two short entries with the page number. The register is in Box 14, Folder 6, at the North Bend County Archive. The survey is in the same collection but filed under School Facilities rather than Education. That label took me a while to find, so include the full location in our notes for next time.

Please send me your thoughts on the length and whether the map fits on the inside spread. I can cut the second paragraph about the register if space is tight, but I would rather keep the quotation and the detail about the pupils arriving from the ferry because those are the parts that connect the records to daily life. I am not asking for a final layout yet, just a sense of whether the story works at about seven hundred words once the captions are added.
